runs.text: We are preparing for agents to perform most of the work
People use, supervise and build AI
Protect the bank against current and future threats

We are preparing for an operating model in which agents perform most work currently done manually. This is the strategic premise for the programme, not a measured forecast or a target for reducing headcount. Roles will evolve so that people can use AI effectively, supervise its work and build and evaluate agents where their responsibilities require it. The purpose remains protecting the bank against current and future threats. Human judgement, cybersecurity expertise and accountability remain essential. This presentation explains the capabilities needed and the priorities for developing them.

Everyone shares a foundation. The rest follows their work.

The model combines four components into a target capability profile. Foundation is shared by everyone in the cyber workforce and is not a fourth agentic level. Choose an agentic level according to how the person will work with agents, then select role specialisms and training on the tools they will use. Role specialisms and tool training can apply at any level. A person may hold several responsibilities. Existing cybersecurity expertise is assumed and must be maintained and enhanced. This diagram describes a capability profile, not a course sequence or an operational permission model.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
Relevant section: The model in one page.
Common understanding for everyone in cyber
Show what AI can do to inspire ideas
Know when and how to check.

Foundation builds a common understanding of both the opportunity and the risks. AI in cyber should show real possibilities, for example investigation and enrichment, code analysis, and policy assessment. The aim is to seed imagination about how work could change, rather than teach a particular product. AI systems and agents covers basic components, tools and actions. Limitations includes hallucination, prompt injection, context loss and automation bias, together with checking habits. Responsible use covers information handling and the bank’s approved-use rules. Threat awareness addresses how attackers use AI and how defence must adapt. Foundation uses the shared outcomes in N1–N5. Third-party vetting in N4.7 and specialist threat tracking in N5.7 sit elsewhere in the model.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
The target follows the work, not seniority
Higher levels build on earlier capabilities. Not everyone needs L3.

The formal labels are L1 Entry, L2 Practitioner and L3 Expert. They describe target agentic capabilities, not seniority or professional expertise. L1 people primarily perform the work themselves and use AI assistance. L2 people supervise agents, adapt task instructions in approved workflows and run task checks. L3 people design agent behaviour, workflows and evaluation approaches. L3 includes no-code and low-code builders. Writing reusable task instructions does not by itself make a person L3. Shared infrastructure and specialist security design belong to the relevant role specialism. Higher levels build on lower shared capabilities, but demonstrated skills need not be retaught. A senior leader can be L1. Capability levels do not grant operational authorisation.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
Relevant section: Agentic levels; The L2/L3 boundary; N6–N11.
Capabilities follow responsibilities, at any agentic level
One person may need specialisms from several roles

These are the nine roles in the current model, shown in source order down each column. They preserve the project’s grouping of ECSF profiles, including explicit IAM and vulnerability and exposure management roles. They are not a new list of official ECSF profiles or a fixed organisational chart. Select outcomes for actual responsibilities; one person can need specialisms across several roles, at any agentic level. Examples include responding to agent incidents, managing agent identities, assessing AI risk and leading workflow transformation. Specialist depth follows the responsibility. A role does not require a new standalone module when shared learning and tool practice already meet its needs. Current ordering places IAM eighth and Leadership ninth.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
Relevant section: Role specialisms — what the job requires.
Anthropic Claude Cowork and Claude Code
Agentic SOC tools, such as Microsoft Sentinel
with Security Copilot, or selected alternatives

AI transformation depends on people having access to suitable agentic tools. General-purpose options include Microsoft Copilot Cowork, Anthropic Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Specialist tools should serve the work of each function, including an agentic SOC; Microsoft Sentinel with Security Copilot is an illustrative option, not a procurement recommendation. Select the tools and establish the deployment timeline, then create dedicated training plans for the tasks and permissions of each audience. Foundation can start earlier. Provide hands-on access during pilots and align product-specific training with deployment so that learning can be applied immediately. The same product can require different training for users, supervisors and builders. No deployment dates or purchase decisions are assumed.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
Relevant section: Tool training; Planning tool training.
The model defines what people learn
Build on what people can already demonstrate

A capability profile specifies the target. Learning needs identify the topics required to reach that target. Learning outcomes state what a person must know or do and allow training resources and realistic exercises to be selected and assessed. Compare target outcomes with demonstrated current capability so that people do not repeat learning unnecessarily. Without a baseline, these are target learning needs, not measured skill gaps. Generic capabilities transfer across functions, such as supervising or evaluating agents. Cyber-specific learning concerns cybersecurity work, threats and controls. These are content categories, independent of level, role and tool access. Generic does not mean everyone must take it, and some cyber-specific awareness has a broad audience. Course coverage, demonstrated competence and operational permission are separate decisions.
Source: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md, version 2, updated 18 October 2026. Authoritative local source: /Users/cyberk/projects/ai-era-training/Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md.
Relevant section: From the model to learning needs; Generic and cyber-specific learning needs; From target work to a training plan.
Coordinate capability development, tools and ways of working

First validate the model and learning needs with the relevant leaders and practitioners. Training selection and tool planning should run in parallel: choose suitable courses and exercises, build missing material, and establish the approved tool roadmap and access dates. Together these inputs determine the audiences, what they learn and when. Define readiness gates and the role of certification before widening use. These are design decisions to develop, not an existing approved certification policy. Distinguish training completion, practical competence and operational authorisation. Pilot and roll out in phases, using evidence from each phase to refine the next. Throughout the programme, address workforce practices: give juniors supervised cases that build independent judgement, maintain core skills with investigations and exercises without AI, form independent assessments before reviewing AI output where appropriate, and rehearse agent failures, takeover and continued operation.
